14.steps:
1) Log in to admin UI.
2) Click to edit the NAT policy.
3) Click the Advanced tab
4) Set probe type to Ping
5) Set NAT method to Round Robin.
6) Click OK
7) Use clients to connect to resources continually.
8) Verify that for each connection new service next service in NAT policy is used.
The round robin remap algorithm sends each incoming connection to the next address in its list. For example, in a 3 server cluster (servers A, B, C), connection #1 would go to server A, connection #2 would go to server B, connection #3 would go to server C, and request #4 would go to server A, thus completing the round robin of all servers.
14.initial: NAT Method Round Robin- source ANY to pool with Address Object containing hosts
14.title: Probe port
14.result: Round robin algorithm behaves as expected.

19.steps:
1) Log in to admin UI.
2) Click to edit the NAT policy.
3) Click the Advanced tab
4) Set probe type to Ping
5) On General tab set NAT method to Sticky IP.
6) Click OK
7) Use clients to connect to resources continually.
8) Verify that for each connection the IP which the client maps to is used.
The sticky IP remap algorithm uses a hash algorithm whereby the source IP address is modulo with the size of the server cluster to determine the server to remap to. For example, in a 3 server cluster (servers A, B, C), the host 192.168.168.100 would remap to server A (192.168.168.100 % 3 = 1).
For this setup:
67.1.2.3 => 10.190.6.106
204.20.30.40 => 10.190.6.105
217.8.9.11 => 10.190.6.107
19.initial: Setup A with NAT policy A.    Capture traffic on port that has the service that will be probed.  Probes enabled.
19.title: NAT Method Sticky IP- source ANY to pool with Address
19.result:
Sticky IP algorithm behaves as expected.

25.steps:
1) Log in to admin UI.
2) Click to edit the NAT policy.
3) Click the Advanced tab
4) Set probe type to Ping
5) Set NAT method to Block Remapping
6) Click OK
7) Use clients to connect to resources continually.
8) Verify that for each connection new service next service in NAT policy is used.
The block remapping algorithm divides the size of the source network by the size of the address pool to create logical segments. For example, where x is a 10.1.1.0/24 source subnet and y is a range of addresses 4.2.2.1 - 4.2.2.8 being used as an outbound pool. The 10.1.1.0/24 subnet will be divided into 32 segments (size of x / size of y), and remap the first 32 of x to the first y (10.1.1.1-10.1.1.31 to 4.2.2.1), the seconds 32 of x to the second y (10.1.1.32-10.1.1.63 to 4.2.2.2) etc.
For this setup:
size of x/size of y = 128/3 = 42 2/3
10.190.16.10 (WebBench Client 1) => 192.168.168.10
10.190.16.72 (WebBench Client 2) => 192.168.168.72
10.190.16.125 (WebBench Client 3) => 192.168.168.125
25.initial: Setup B with NAT policy C.    Capture traffic on port that has the service that will be probed.  Probes enabled.
25.title: NAT Method Block remapping - source Network to pool with Address Object containing range
25.result: Block Remapping algorithm behaves as expected.

29.steps:
1) Log in to admin UI.
2) Click to edit the NAT policy.
3) Click the Advanced tab
4) Set NAT method to Symmetrical Mapping
5) Click OK
6) Use clients to connect to resources continually.
7) Verify that for each connection the correct mapping is used.
This algorithm grafts the network portion of the pool addresses over the top of the address that is being modified. For example, if the address pool is 192.0.2.0/25 and the address being modified is 10.0.0.50, then the resulting address will be 192.0.2.50. If the address pool is 192.0.2.0/25, and the address being modified is 10.0.0.130, then the resultant address will be 192.0.2.2.
For this setup:
10.190.16.10 (WebBench Client 1) => 192.168.168.10
10.190.16.72 (WebBench Client 2) => 192.168.168.72
10.190.16.125 (WebBench Client 3) => 192.168.168.125
